2015 से ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की बढ़ी रफ्तार, शोधकर्ताओं ने किया खुलासा
वैज्ञानिकों ने पाया है कि 2015 के आसपास से ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की रफ्तार बढ़ गई है, जिसमें तापमान 0.35 डिग्री सेल्सियस प्रति दशक की दर से बढ़ रहा है। ...और पढ़ें
HighLights
2015 के बाद ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की रफ्तार में वृद्धि।
तापमान अब 0.35°C प्रति दशक की दर से बढ़ा।
कई वैज्ञानिक डेटासेट ने इस त्वरण की पुष्टि की।
डिजिटल डेस्क, वॉशिंगटन। विज्ञानियों ने पता लगाया है कि ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की रफ्तार बढ़ गई है। 2015 के आसपास से ग्लोबल वार्मिंग की रफ़्तार बढ़ी है। पाट्सडैम इंस्टीट्यूट फार क्लाइमेट इंपैक्ट रिसर्च (पीआइके) के विश्लेषण के आधार पर विज्ञानियों ने यह दावा किया है।
शोधकर्ताओं का कहना है कि दुनिया का तापमान लगभग 0.35° डिग्री सेल्सियस प्रति दशक की अनुमानित रफ़्तार से बढ़ रहा है। 1970 से 2015 के बीच तापमान बढ़ने की औसत दर 0.2°डिग्री सेल्सियस प्रति दशक से थोड़ी कम थी। यह अध्ययन वैज्ञानिक जर्नल जियोफिजिकल रिसर्च लेटर्स में प्रकाशित हुआ है।
साइंस डेली की रिपोर्ट के अनुसार, अमेरिकी सांख्यिकी विशेषज्ञ और इस अध्ययन के सह-लेखक ग्रांट फोस्टर ने कहा, हम 2015 के आसपास से ग्लोबल वार्मिंग में तेजी आई है।
तापमान के सभी पांचों रिकार्ड में एक जैसा ही पैटर्न दिखा, भले ही ये डाटा अलग-अलग वैज्ञानिक संगठनों ने तैयार किए थे और इनमें अलग-अलग तरीकों का इस्तेमाल किया गया था। सभी डेटासेट में ग्लोबल वार्मिंग में 2013 या 2014 में दिखने लगी थी। शोधकर्ता इस बड़े बदलाव की शुरुआत 2015 के आसपास मानते हैं, जब इसके साक्ष्य स्पष्ट हुए।

South Korea sizzles at 42.5°C amid heatwave, hottest day in 122 years
South Korea's weather agency warned temperatures could rise further in western regions this week and said the heatwave and tropical nights were likely to persist.
A record heatwave is gripping the Korean Peninsula, sending temperatures soaring across South Korea and North Korea as authorities expand emergency measures and residents seek relief in cooling shelters, beaches and water parks.
Forecasters said on Monday that extreme heat, previously concentrated in South Korea's southeast, was spreading to the Seoul metropolitan area and other western regions. North Korean state media also reported temperatures approaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in parts of the country and a fifth straight tropical night in Pyongyang.
South Korea's weather agency warned temperatures could rise further in western regions this week and said the heatwave and tropical nights were likely to persist.
Data released by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency on Sunday showed that 14 had died and 1,889 people had suffered heat-related illnesses since mid-May.
The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said Yangsan recorded 42.5 C on Sunday, the highest temperature measured in 122 years of weather observations. The southeastern city had already broken the national record on the two preceding days.
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook ordered ministries and local governments to mobilise all available resources to respond to heatwave and drought risks after the government raised its heatwave response alert to the second-highest level, unlocking funding for relief efforts and more frequent inspections in affected areas.
Power authorities have activated emergency measures and are closely monitoring supply and demand as electricity consumption is expected to reach a record high in late August amid surging air-conditioning use.
The KMA on Monday issued its first-ever severe heatwave warning for parts of Seoul and neighbouring Gyeonggi Province, while the same highest-level heat alerts remained in effect across southern regions including Busan, Ulsan, South Gyeongsang and parts of Gwangju and South Jeolla Province.
BASEBALL GAMES CANCELLED
Local governments have scrambled to protect vulnerable residents. Seoul districts have expanded cooling shelters and distributed free water and sun umbrellas, while Yangsan has expanded water-spraying operations and water distribution.
Searing temperatures have disrupted daily life. Over the weekend, the Korea Baseball Organisation cancelled games in Busan and Changwon and said further schedule adjustments could be considered if dangerous conditions persist.
Local media reported packed beaches, water parks and riverside recreation areas.
At Seoul's Cheonggyecheon stream, where the city is running a summer water festival featuring temporary paddling zones and splash areas, families sought relief from the heat.
"Forty degrees is not a number we used to see in Korea, but now it feels like we see it all the time," said Park Jin-woo, 39, who brought his children there to cool down.
Seoul resident Lee Jub-young, 43, said the heat had made parasols a necessity rather than a fashion accessory.
"This climate crisis has become something citizens can feel on their own skin," he said.
North Korea is experiencing similar conditions. State media said heat advisories covering much of the country would remain in place through the week and reported that tens of thousands of people visited the Wonsan Kalma Coastal Tourist Zone during July.
Water parks in Pyongyang were also packed, according to state television.

Heat wave spreads as Seoul nears 38 degrees Celsius, South Jeolla heat index hits 40C
Extreme heat is expanding westward, with Seoul nearing 38 degrees Celsius, southern regions facing life-threatening conditions and Typhoon Dolphin adding uncertainty.
A pedestrian uses a sun umbrella to shield against the heat while crossing a street in Seoul on Aug. 3.NEWS1
Extreme heat is expected to spread farther west on Monday, sending daytime highs in the Seoul metropolitan area to as high as 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit).
The heat index is also expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius in parts of South Jeolla.
"Daytime highs on Monday are expected to range from 33 to 39 degrees Celsius, similar to Sunday," the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said. "Temperatures in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang are expected to exceed 39 degrees Celsius, bringing extreme heat at life-threatening levels."
Yangsan in South Gyeongsang, which set a new national temperature record of 42.5 degrees Celsius on Sunday, had already reached 37.9 degrees Celsius by 11 a.m. Monday.
The Yeongnam region — the area encompassing Busan, Ulsan, Gyeongsang provinces and Daegu — where temperatures have exceeded 40 degrees Celsius for five consecutive days, is likely to exceed that mark again.
Heat index hits 40 degrees in Yeosu
Temperatures in regions west of the Taebaek mountain range are expected to rise significantly from Monday as easterly winds cross the mountains and warm through compressional heating before descending on the western side.
The KMA issued its highest-level extreme heat emergency warning for eastern Gwangju and cities of Boseong, Yeosu, Gwangyang, Suncheon and Gokseong in South Jeolla. Gwangju is forecast to reach 39 degrees Celsius during the day, while the heat index in Yeosu is expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius.
"People should suspend all nonessential outdoor activities and work whenever possible, and move to cool places such as shaded areas, heat shelters or air-conditioned facilities to rest and stay hydrated," a KMA official said.
Seoul is expected to reach a daytime high of 37 degrees Celsius, more than 2 degrees higher than Sunday's 34.9 degrees Celsius. Some parts of the metropolitan area could exceed 38 degrees Celsius.
"Stronger easterly winds could push temperatures even higher in the metropolitan area, prompting some heat advisories to be upgraded to warnings or the issuance of the highest-level extreme heat emergency warning," the KMA said.
Scattered showers are expected across parts of the southern regions on Tuesday, likely easing the heat wave that has pushed temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius. However, daytime highs are still expected to remain around 37 degrees Celsius, and the heat index could climb after the rain because of high humidity.
Dolphin's path could worsen or ease the heat wave
Typhoon Dolphin, the year's 13th named storm, is another factor that could affect the heat wave.
As of 9 a.m. Monday, Dolphin was moving west-northwest at 18 kilometers per hour (11 miles per hour) over waters about 1,520 kilometers (944 miles) east of Okinawa, Japan. It had a central pressure of 940 millibars and maximum sustained winds of 47 meters (154 feet) per second, maintaining a Level 4 intensity on the KMA's five-tier scale.
The typhoon is forecast to pass over Okinawa on Friday as it continues westward, though its path afterward remains highly uncertain. If it continues toward China, it is expected to strengthen easterly winds, worsening the heat wave.
There is also a possibility that the storm could turn north and directly affect Korea. While that could help ease the heat wave and drought conditions, it could also bring typhoon-related damage.
"Temperatures and rainfall patterns may change depending on the typhoon's track and surrounding atmospheric conditions," the KMA said.
BY CHON KWON-PIL [lee.taehee2@joongang.co.kr]

South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to “immediately” stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.
The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5C on Sunday afternoon, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said, the highest temperature reported since modern weather observation began in 1904.
Yangsan has been the centre of an ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40C for a fifth consecutive day on Sunday, while many other cities including Daegu and Busan are seeing temperatures climb into the high 30s.
People gathered in airconditioned shopping malls or cafes to escape the blistering temperatures. Others sought relief under mist-spray zones set up in Seoul. Ju Dong-yeol, 27, took refuge from the heat in a Starbucks in the South Korean capital, along with his parents and told AFP “it is too hot to be outside doing anything”.
“I can’t think of anything else to do other than stay in airconditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafes,” the office worker said.
The city of Gyeongju, about 240km south-east of Seoul, reached 40.3C on Sunday, its highest recorded temperature in eight years.
North Korea has also faced punishing heat, with temperatures soaring as high as 40C in some regions, state media reported on Monday. Residents in Pyongyang have endured a week of nights where the temperature has not dropped below 25C.
More than 20 localities in South Korea were under emergency heatwave alerts on Sunday – a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38C or an actual temperature of 39C for the day.
Issuing a heat warning, the weather agency urged people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, adding that “indoor spaces without air conditioning are dangerous”.
“Move immediately to a cool place, such as a designated cooling centre or a shaded area, and stay hydrated while resting,” it advised.
Fearing for those people most vulnerable to heat, the prime minister, Han Seong-sook, ordered local officials to strengthen safety checks on residents and to ensure a stable power and water supply was maintained.
Easterly winds are expected to push the extreme heat further inland on Monday, with Seoul forecast to reach 37C. “Temperatures in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang are expected to exceed 39C, bringing extreme heat at life-threatening levels,” the KMA said.
Officials are also monitoring Typhoon Dolphin, which is now tracking towards China’s south-east coastal regions, south of the Korean peninsula, and could dictate how long the stifling heat persists.
If the typhoon moves towards eastern China, it could increase humidity and potentially worsening the heatwave and tropical nights in Korea, the KMA said. But a path closer to the south of the peninsula could bring stronger winds, greater cloud cover and rain, temporarily easing the heat.
KMA data show the average annual number of heatwave days in the country has more than doubled to 19 in the past five years.
A heatwave day is defined as one with a maximum temperature of at least 33C.
South Korea’s professional baseball league was forced to cancel one game in Changwon after the city’s temperature climbed to 39.5C, marking the second consecutive game cancellation in the city.
“The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority, as a severe heatwave warning remains in effect for the Changwon area,” said the Korea Baseball Organization in a statement.
Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.
Adding to the extreme weather is the return this year of El Niño – a natural climate phenomenon that warms Pacific Ocean surface temperatures and typically occurs every two to seven years.
With Agence France-Presse

As extreme heat becomes an increasingly serious occupational hazard, Japanese companies are exploring unconventional cooling technologies that go beyond fans and portable air conditioners. One of the latest innovations attracting global attention is the Do Hiemon Box, a human-sized cooling booth designed to rapidly lower body temperature after prolonged exposure to heat.
Developed by Japanese refrigeration and vending machine manufacturer SDRS and distributed by industrial equipment supplier TRUSCO Nakayama, the product is less of a refrigerator in the traditional sense and more of a mobile recovery station for workers operating in high-temperature environments.
A Cooling Booth Inspired by Japan’s Vending Machines
At first glance, the Do Hiemon Box resembles an oversized refrigerated vending machine. The design inspiration is intentional: Japan’s ubiquitous refrigerated vending machines are engineered to maintain stable temperatures efficiently, and SDRS has adapted similar cooling technology into a booth large enough for one person.
The system focuses on rapidly reducing an individual’s body temperature. Users step inside, sit on an integrated chair, and receive targeted streams of chilled air directed toward the head, neck, shoulders, and back—the areas most effective for dissipating body heat.
How the Do Hiemon Box Works
The booth maintains an internal ambient temperature of approximately 15°C, while colder air around 5°C is blown through strategically positioned vents. According to SDRS, users can begin feeling noticeably cooler within five minutes, while a session of around 10 minutes may help alleviate symptoms associated with heat exhaustion after prolonged outdoor work.
To ensure safe operation, the booth includes:
- Three adjustable cooling modes with different airflow patterns
- Automatic shut-off after 20 minutes to prevent excessive cooling
- Lockable caster wheels, allowing the unit to be relocated as needed
Built for Construction Sites, Factories, and Outdoor Events
The Do Hiemon Box is intended primarily for industrial and commercial settings where workers are regularly exposed to high temperatures.
Potential applications include:
Because the unit requires no permanent installation and operates from a standard electrical outlet, businesses can deploy it wherever temporary cooling stations are needed.
Energy-Efficient Alternative to Spot Cooling
One of the product’s notable selling points is energy efficiency. SDRS says the booth consumes roughly 0.51 kWh, approximately half the electricity required by a conventional spot air conditioner. Operating costs are estimated at 16 yen per hour, making it a practical solution for employers looking to provide rapid cooling without significantly increasing electricity consumption.
Developed in Response to Rising Heat Risks
Japan has experienced increasingly severe summers, with recurring heatstroke warnings and record-breaking temperatures placing pressure on employers to improve worker safety. The Do Hiemon Box reflects a growing shift toward dedicated heat mitigation technologies rather than relying solely on hydration breaks and shade.
Instead of replacing conventional cooling systems, the booth serves as a recovery station that allows overheated workers to quickly reduce their core temperature before returning to work, helping minimize the risk of heat-related illnesses.
Price and Availability
The Do Hiemon Box is currently available in Japan through TRUSCO Nakayama’s industrial distribution network. The standard unit is priced at approximately 1.5 million yen (around US$9,000–10,000, depending on exchange rates), positioning it as an investment for businesses and public facilities rather than individual consumers. One unit has also been installed at Maebashi City Hall for public use during periods of extreme heat.
A Glimpse Into Climate-Responsive Workplace Technology
While its refrigerator-like appearance has generated viral attention online, the Do Hiemon Box represents a broader trend in climate-adaptive workplace technology. As heatwaves become more frequent worldwide, industries are increasingly exploring specialized cooling infrastructure to protect workers in environments where conventional air conditioning is impractical.
The Do Hiemon Box highlights how targeted cooling systems could become an important component of occupational safety in an era of rising global temperatures.

Seoul and parts of Gyeonggi Province came under the capital region’s first Heat Wave Emergency Warning on Monday, as record-breaking heat in southeastern South Korea spread westward.
The Korea Meteorological Administration issued the warning at 4 p.m. for Tuesday, when the daily maximum perceived temperature is expected to exceed 38 degrees Celsius and the daytime high is forecast to surpass 39 C.
The warning, the highest level in the KMA’s heat alert system, applies to all Seoul districts south of the Han River, including Gangnam-gu, as well as Osan, Hanam and western Yeoju in Gyeonggi Province.
Introduced this year, the Heat Wave Emergency Warning signals exceptionally dangerous conditions in which even healthy people face a sharply increased risk of serious heat-related illness or death, KMA Administrator Lee Mi-seon said.
Under the warning, authorities strongly recommend suspending nonessential outdoor work and moving to air-conditioned indoor spaces or cooling shelters. They also advise stepped-up safety checks on vulnerable households.
The highest-level warning had previously been issued mainly in southeastern areas, particularly South Gyeongsang Province, after Yangsan recorded a national high of 42.5 C on Sunday.
The KMA attributed the westward spread of the heat to easterly winds carrying hot air toward the capital region.
High temperatures are also expected to persist overnight and in the coming days.
“As heat accumulated during the day continues into the night, we urge residents in the metropolitan area to regularly check the latest weather information and take extra precautions, including staying hydrated and getting sufficient rest,” a KMA official said.

NNA – The Ministry of Agriculture, through the Lebanese Agricultural Research Institute (LARI), has issued safety guidelines to help cope with the ongoing severe heatwave and reduce the risk of wildfires, as high temperatures are expected to persist until mid-August.
The ministry explained that these precautionary measures aim to protect citizens and farmers, safeguard property and agricultural areas, and minimize the risk of fires in forested and agricultural regions. The move is part of efforts to promote environmental protection, raise public awareness, and strengthen coordination among relevant authorities.
As weather forecasts point to temperatures remaining above seasonal averages, reaching 40°C in the Bekaa Valley and 35°C along the coast, with nighttime temperatures also expected to remain elevated, reaching 30°C in the Bekaa, the risk of fires rises to critical levels the ministry continued to indicate.
In its issued guidelines, the Agriculture Ministry made the following recommendations:
-For citizens: staying hydrated, wearing protective hats and sunglasses, using sunscreen, avoiding direct sun exposure during peak hours (11 a.m. to 4 p.m.), and not leaving children or flammable items such as lighters inside vehicles exposed to heat.
-Avoiding mobile phone use while refueling, checking household electrical connections, staying in shaded or air-conditioned areas, and taking precautions with food storage during high temperatures.
-Drivers are advised to monitor vehicle water and oil levels, avoid excessive braking on mountain roads, and refrain from throwing cigarette butts in natural areas to prevent fires.
-For farmers: avoiding the use of fertilizers and pesticides during the heatwave, maintaining regular irrigation where water is available, cooling greenhouses and poultry farms, and refraining from burning grass or other materials without strict supervision.
-For authorities and emergency teams: regularly clearing dry grass along roadsides, ensuring fires from outdoor activities are fully extinguished, preparing water tanks and firefighting equipment, reporting smoke or early signs of fires, and ensuring rapid response teams are ready for emergencies.
The Agriculture Ministry also called on municipalities to provide water tankers equipped with pumps to regularly spray roads and public areas to help reduce temperatures and support fire prevention efforts.

Ulsan's factories fight the summer swelter with ice machines, cooling vests and chilled fruit punch
As longer, harsher summers grip Korea’s industrial hub, shipyards and plants are expanding breaks, cooling gear and heat safeguards to prevent illness.
Workers at LS MnM's Onsan plant work through the heat in Ulsan.LS MNM
Workers poured out of the HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) shipyard in Dong District, Ulsan, at about 6 p.m. on July 24 — the end of a workday that had peaked at 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit). They had stripped off their overalls and changed into shorts and short sleeves, and the day of heat and labor showed on their faces.
"Wring out your overalls by hand, and sweat pours out of them," said a worker surnamed Kim, who works on the yard floor. "You can just assume I spent the whole day soaked."
The surface of a ship's steel plating exceeds 50 degrees Celsius in the summer sun. Welders work close to flames above 1,200 degrees Celsius. Once workers don their overalls, safety boots, hard hat and goggles, their underwear is soaked through within minutes.
"When break time comes, the first place I go is wherever the company has put an air conditioner, and I lie down," he said. "The heat started late this summer, but what my body is feeling is much worse than other years."
Shipyards, car plants, refining and petrochemical complexes and smelters across Ulsan are lengthening breaks and adding cooling equipment to head off heat-related illnesses. Ice water, cooling vests, chilled fruit punch and restorative meals have all been pressed into service.
HD HHI has extended its lunch break by 30 minutes through Aug. 31. When the apparent temperature reaches 33 degrees Celsius, rest periods double to 20 minutes from 10 as per the legal requirements.The company has built separate rest areas on board ships and runs about 270 shelters in all, including converted buses, shade canopies and the pop-up structures Koreans call "Mongolian tents." It has added ice machines and portable air conditioners, and hands out ice water, salt and glucose tablets and fan-equipped vests. A "roving snack truck" serving 1,000 portions at a time of hwachae, a chilled fruit punch, will run until early September.
Refiners and petrochemical producers, who work with hot oil and gas year-round, have also stepped up their own measures.
SK Ulsan CLX, the country's largest refining and petrochemical production base, adds 10 minutes of rest an hour when a heat wave advisory is issued and 15 minutes under a heat wave warning.
A heat advisory is issued when the daily maximum apparent temperature is forecast to remain at or above 33 degrees Celsius. A heat wave emergency warning is issued when an area has already endured at least two straight days with an apparent temperature of 35 degrees Celsius or higher and is expected to experience an apparent temperature of at least 38 degrees Celsius for a day or a daytime high of 39 degrees Celsius or above.
Ice water and salt tablets are kept near work areas, and cooling clothing and ice pack vests are mandatory. When a heat wave warning is in effect, the plant avoids work between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. when it can and shifts tasks to early morning or overnight.
"We check workers' body temperature and general condition at frequent intervals," a company representative said.
S-Oil's Ulsan plant issues cups of ice, sports drinks and heat kits, and serves restorative dishes such as samgyetang, a ginseng chicken soup, along with watermelon once a week. LS MnM's Onsan smelter, which runs furnaces above 1,200 degrees Celsius, keeps ice cream, vitamins and salt and glucose tablets on site. Above a set temperature, it messages every employee with reminders to drink water and rest, and halts outdoor work when necessary. Hyundai Motor's Ulsan plant runs ice machines along its production lines and serves restorative dishes and frozen desserts daily.
The spending reflects a summer that keeps getting longer. Analysis by the Ulsan Research Institute of Korea Meteorological Administration data put the city at 121 summer days last year. The count measures stretches in which the daily mean temperature held at 20 degrees Celsius or above. That is 16 days more than in 1995 and 23 more than in 1975. Heat wave days and tropical nights are both trending upward.
A tropical night refers to a phenomenon when nighttime temperatures stay above 25 degrees Celcius.
The longer season is affecting workers' health. Ulsan recorded 17.2 cases of heat-related illnesses per 100,000 residents last year, the second-highest rate in the country, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency figures show. The concentration of factories and outdoor worksites in the city leaves unusually large numbers of workers exposed.
The heat also produces one of Ulsan's more particular sights. Large employers, including HD HHI and Hyundai Motor, take their collective summer break at the same time — at the end of July and the start of August. The industrial city empties as about 300,000 of Ulsan's 1.1 million residents are Hyundai employees and their families. Many local businesses shut down alongside them, and some city bus routes run reduced services.
The city government is building infrastructure to reduce the toll of the summer heat. Through a central government competition, it plans to develop a disaster safety industry facility equipped with an artificial climate chamber, where safety products and technologies designed for extreme heat can be tested, evaluated and certified. It also intends to work with the heat wave research center at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology on AI-based localized heat data and response technology tailored to industrial sites.
"With climate change, heat has moved past seasonal discomfort and become a disaster that threatens safety on industrial sites," Kim Hye-rin, a researcher at the center, said.
"On shipbuilding, automotive and petrochemical sites, radiant heat piles on top of an already hot and humid environment, so the 'perceived' temperature is higher and the risk of heat illness is greater. That calls for more than longer breaks. It needs a comprehensive system covering adjusted working hours, expanded cooling equipment and real-time heat risk management."

China warns of crop risks as heatwave sweeps agricultural regions
Sustained high temperatures may crimp yields while high humidity could raise risks of crop diseases
[HONG KONG] China’s corn, rice and cotton fields are at heightened risk of crop damage in the coming days as a heatwave sweeps through key agricultural regions in the country’s north and east.
High pressure weather systems will lead to hotter-than-normal conditions this week, according to commercial forecaster Vaisala, with Shenyang in the northeastern province of Liaoning seeing highs of 35 to 38 degree Celsius through Thursday (Aug 6).
Beijing will hit the low- to mid-30 degree Celsius range into the weekend.
The provincial climate centre for Shandong, which accounts for 10 per cent of China’s corn production, warned last week that sustained temperatures in the mid- to high- 30 degree Celsius range through at least Wednesday may crimp yields of the summer corn crop.
High humidity caused by moist monsoonal flows could also raise the risk of crop diseases, it added.
Further north, officials in Liaoning – which contributes some 7 per cent of national corn output – have also expressed concern.
“Major crops such as corn and rice are currently in their critical growth stages, and soil moisture loss is accelerating on sloping hills and sandy areas,” the city government of Jinzhou, a city in the province, said on Jul 31.
Separately, Vaisala meteorologist Kyle Tapley also said there was potential for heat stress on corn and soybean crops in Liaoning and Inner Mongolia.
Scorching heat is set to take hold in Xinjiang too, the autonomous region of northwest China where almost all of the country’s cotton is grown.
In an early warning notice last week, the regional climate centre forecast widespread temperatures of at least 35 degree Celsius through Aug 11, with Turpan, southeast of the regional capital Urumqi, hitting as high as 50 degree Celsius.
“Sustained high temperatures could negatively impact corn grain filling, cotton boll growth and fruit enlargement, leading to stunted development, sunburn and premature ripening,” the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Climate Center said in a bulletin.
The ongoing heat and drought may cut Xinjiang’s cotton production by as much as 5 per cent in August, according to commercial forecaster Marcus Weather.
Not only China has been affected by the latest heat wave. In South Korea, the highest temperature on record – 42.5 degree Celsius – was reported over the weekend in the southeastern city of Yangsan.
Fruit enlargement has slowed somewhat at some pear orchards in Ulsan, while fruit shrivelling occurred at some grape orchards with poor drainage, according to a statement by the Rural Development Administration of South Korea.
While the north of China swelters, the country’s southern provinces – where soils are already saturated from weeks of wetter-than-normal weather – are set to see rains drag on in the coming days.
In particular, Guangdong and Guangxi are set to see heavy rain this week, heightening the risk of rice blast disease in the south of the country, the China Meteorological Administration said in a bulletin published over the weekend. BLOOMBERG

In short:
Authorities in South Korea have told residents to immediately stop all outdoor activities amid an extreme heatwave.
It comes as the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded the country's hottest temperature on record, at 42.5C.
What's next?
Meanwhile, Japan invented a new term — "kokushobi", meaning "cruelly hot day" — for temperatures over 40C. Ongoing heat conditions have impacted earthquake rescue efforts.
South Korea yesterday registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to "immediately" stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.
The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the thermometer reach 42.5 degrees Celsius at 1:26 pm local time, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said on its website.
Yangsan has been the epicentre of the ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40C for a fifth consecutive day yesterday, while many other cities, including Daegu and Busan, have been sweltering in the high 30s.
People flocked to air-conditioned shopping malls or cafes to escape the blistering heat, an AFP reporter saw.
Ju Dong-yeol, 27, took refuge in a Starbucks in Seoul along with his parents and told AFP: "It is too hot to be outside doing anything.
"I can't think of anything else to do other than stay in air-conditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafes,"the office worker said.
South Korea's professional baseball league was also forced to cancel a game in Changwon after the city's temperature climbed to 39.5 degrees Celsius during the day, marking the second consecutive game cancellation in the city.
"The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority, as a severe heatwave warning remains in effect for the Changwon area," said the Korea Baseball Organisation in a statement.
More than 20 localities were under emergency heatwave alerts yesterday — a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures.
An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38C or an actual temperature of 39C for the day.
Japan's 'cruel' new heat category
South Korea is not the only country in the region introducing new categories for extreme heat.
Japan experienced its first "kokushobi", or "cruelly hot day", late last month.
The term was introduced in April this year for days where the mercury hits more than 40C.
The ongoing heat in Japan hampered rescue efforts from a devastating 7.1-magnitude last week, which killed 38 people.
About 95,000 homes were without water as of Friday, amid heatwave conditions, and officials warned of heat stroke risk.
Rescue authorities said lack of power and running water was a concern in the punishing heat.
Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.
Adding to the extreme weather is the return this year of El Nino — a natural climate phenomenon that warms the surface of the Pacific Ocean and typically occurs every two to seven years.
Europe has also sweltered through a scorching summer this year, with prolonged heatwaves pushing temperatures above 40C in parts of the south.
European authorities issued health warnings, battled wildfires and urged people to avoid outdoor activities during afternoons.
After sweeping across western Europe at the start of last week, the season's latest heatwave scorched central Europe before reaching Italy over the weekend.
Italian authorities said nearly all of the country's major cities would be under the highest heat alert from today.

In the wake of a recent earthquake that hit southwestern Japan's Kumamoto Prefecture, lifelines remain cut off and extreme heat has added to the hardship. Amid such circumstances, many people are taking shelter in evacuation centers. Every possible effort must be made to protect their lives.
The quake, which measured a full 7 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale, caused houses to collapse in various areas, raising concerns that evacuation will drag on. Living in harsh conditions heightens the risk of physical illness, and stress and deterioration of living conditions could lead to disaster-related deaths.
Unlike direct deaths caused by collapsed buildings and other immediate damage, disaster-related deaths can be prevented if appropriate support is provided. Yet during the Kumamoto earthquakes 10 years ago, such deaths accounted for 80% of the 278 fatalities. Even in the Noto Peninsula earthquake in 2024, the deaths of 520 people -- close to 70% of the total number of fatalities -- were deemed to be disaster-related.
This time, particular attention needs to be paid to heatstroke countermeasures. Across the Kyushu region, days of intense heat with temperatures of 35 degrees Celsius or above are continuing. Spending time or doing cleanup work in environments without air conditioning can be life-threatening. It is essential to spread awareness of preventive measures.
People should hydrate and take in salt frequently and spend time in air-conditioned places. If the power is out, they should open windows and entrances to create airflow and block sunlight with curtains or other coverings. Placing a wet towel on the skin and fanning it makes it easier for heat to escape from the body.
Efforts to improve conditions in evacuation centers are also being put to the test.

Water isn't enough: What to eat and drink to survive extreme heat
Hot weather has arrived, with temperatures expected to reach as high as 37°C in some areas.
How to survive the extreme heat is explained by dietitian Oksana Skytalinska.
A global health threat
Heat is no longer just a temporary discomfort - it has become a real challenge for humanity. According to the latest The Lancet Countdown report, extreme temperatures claim one human life every minute worldwide.
As the planet continues to warm rapidly, simple protective measures are becoming a matter of basic survival.
When the thermometer keeps climbing, our bodies begin working at the limit of their capabilities. Sweating is the body's primary defense against overheating.
However, excessive sweating causes us to lose not only vital fluids but also essential minerals, particularly potassium and sodium, which doctors refer to as electrolytes.
These electrolytes are responsible for keeping the heart functioning properly, supporting the nervous system, and maintaining a healthy fluid balance in every cell of the body. Replacing these losses should be a top priority for everyone.
Proper hydration and recovery
Many people mistakenly believe that drinking a glass of ice-cold water is enough to quench their thirst, but in reality, that's not sufficient. If you're sweating heavily while working outdoors or walking around the city, plain water alone cannot fully restore your body's electrolyte balance.
Doctors strongly recommend including medicinal mineral water or pharmacy oral rehydration solutions in your diet. Even a small portion of salty food can help quickly replace dangerous sodium losses.
One of the best indicators of dehydration is the color of your urine. A light straw-colored shade indicates proper hydration, while darker urine is a serious warning sign of dehydration.
Weakly brewed green tea is another excellent option for cooling your body from the inside. Coffee lovers should be especially careful and always drink an additional large glass of water after every cup of coffee.
Sugary soft drinks should never be used to quench your thirst. Their high sugar content only increases thirst, while providing almost none of the beneficial minerals your body needs.
A summer diet for easier digestion
What you eat during hot weather directly affects your ability to tolerate high temperatures. Heavy and fatty meals force your body to spend a tremendous amount of energy breaking down and digesting food.
This process generates additional heat inside the body, making you feel even more uncomfortable. That's why meat dishes are best left for late evening, after the sun has completely set.
During the day, choose foods that are rich in potassium. Add fresh tomatoes, crunchy celery, leafy greens, ripe avocados, sweet kiwis, juicy apricots, melon, and legumes to your daily menu.
Cold soups such as Spanish gazpacho, traditional beet soup, or light okroshka made with whey are ideal choices.
Interestingly, mint and menthol-containing products do not actually lower your body temperature, but they effectively activate cold-sensitive receptors, creating a refreshing sensation of coolness.
Sun safety and external cooling
In addition to eating and drinking properly, it's important to create comfortable conditions for your body from the outside as well.
The simplest rule is to avoid direct sunlight during the hottest part of the day, from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
If you absolutely have to go outside, wear only light-colored, loose-fitting clothing made from thin natural cotton. Never forget a hat, or use a regular sun umbrella, which can significantly reduce heat exposure.
Throughout the day, keep your skin hydrated. Spray your face, neck, and hands with water from a spray bottle, or place a clean, damp cloth on the back of your neck. The human brain is extremely sensitive to overheating, making timely cooling of the neck especially important.
At home, take cool showers regularly, but avoid ice-cold water. Extremely cold water causes blood vessels to constrict sharply, which paradoxically reduces heat loss and prevents your body from cooling itself efficiently.
Finally, try to get enough sleep every night, as good-quality sleep makes your body's natural temperature-regulation mechanisms much stronger and more effective.

EXCELSIOR SPRINGS, Mo. — As summer temperatures soar, Tina Cook, director of risk and regulatory compliance at Excelsior Springs Hospital, recently shared information about preventing heat-related illnesses and dehydration with attendees at the Senior Center inside the Excelsior Springs Community Center.
Heat-related illnesses occur when the body becomes too hot and cannot cool itself properly. High temperatures, humidity, and physical activity can increase the risk.
Cook said overheating can lead to three primary conditions: heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heatstroke.
“Heatstroke is considered a medical emergency,” Cook said.
During heatstroke, a person’s body temperature can become dangerously high. Sweating may stop, and the person may become confused or lose consciousness.
Heat exhaustion is also serious. Symptoms can include heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, cold or clammy skin, and a fast or weak pulse.
Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms that typically occur in the legs, arms, or abdomen. They can develop after heavy sweating causes the body to lose salt and fluids.
Dehydration is separate from heat illness, although the two conditions can occur together. It develops when the body does not have enough fluid to function properly or loses water and electrolytes, including sodium and potassium, through sweating and urination.
“What happens when we get dehydrated is that those electrolytes, sodium, potassium, and water, all get out of balance,” Cook said. “It can make you feel weak. It can make you feel dizzy. It can make you feel nauseated.”
Who Is Most at Risk?
Although anyone can develop heat illness or dehydration, Cook said some people face a greater risk, including:
Adults 65 and older
People with chronic illnesses, including heart disease, kidney conditions, and diabetes
People taking medications that can contribute to dehydration
Individuals with limited mobility
People who live alone
Recognizing the Warning Signs
Cook encouraged residents who spend time outdoors to watch for early warning signs in themselves and others.
Signs of heat illness and dehydration can include:
Muscle cramps
Weakness, dizziness, or faintness
Nausea
Dry mouth or lips
Dark yellow urine
Fatigue
Headache
Confusion or unusual behavior
Residents should call 911 when someone develops severe symptoms, particularly confusion, fainting, a rapid heartbeat, or an inability to cool down.
“Call 911, especially if you live by yourself,” Cook said. “If you or someone you know is starting to feel confused or experiencing dizziness, you’re getting really hot, or you notice your pulse or heart rate starting to rapidly beat, don’t wait.”
Cook said residents should not worry that they are overreacting when symptoms could indicate a medical emergency.
“It’s better to call and be safe rather than be sorry,” she said.
Practical Ways to Prevent Heat Illness
Heat illness is largely preventable when people consistently take steps to remain hydrated and avoid becoming overheated, Cook said.

[Sportschosun Reporter Jang Jong-ho] As intense heat continues across the country, there have been a growing number of deaths from heat-related illnesses.
According to the Central Disaster and Safety Countermeasures Headquarters (CDSCHQ) under the Ministry of the Interior and Safety on the 2nd, 96 people were reported to have suffered heat-related illnesses the previous day.
As a result, the total number of heat-related illness cases reported to the Heat-Related Illness Emergency Room Surveillance System this year rose to 1,889 from May 15 through the previous day, while cumulative deaths reached 14. Heat-related illness is often thought of as nothing more than feeling overheated, but if symptoms are endured or the body remains exposed to heat without proper action, it can become life-threatening, so special caution is needed.
Heat-related illness is an acute condition caused by exposure to excessive heat. Major examples include heat stroke, heat exhaustion and heat cramps. According to the KDCA's Heat-Related Illness Emergency Room Surveillance System, 4,460 people suffered heat-related illness in 2025, about 20% more than the 3,704 cases in 2024. As the heat wave drags on and intensifies, the health damage caused by heat-related illness is also increasing, making it important to respond quickly from the early stages rather than trying to endure the symptoms.
With help from Kim Jeong-yun, head of the regional emergency medical center at Korea University Guro Hospital, we have summarized the symptoms of heat-related illness and the proper ways to respond.
◇Heat-related illness becomes more dangerous the more you endure it... Heat stroke is the deadliest
Heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency that occurs when the hypothalamus, the body's temperature-control center, breaks down. It is marked by a body temperature above 40 degrees Celsius and altered consciousness. Symptoms may include a rapid pulse, low blood pressure, severe headache, chills and confusion. In severe cases, it can lead to multiple organ failure and death, making it the most fatal form of heat-related illness.
Heat-related illness often begins with relatively mild symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea, muscle cramps and extreme fatigue. For that reason, people may dismiss it as simple overheating or try to push through the symptoms until they finish what they are doing. But if they remain in a hot environment, the body's temperature-regulation system can fail, causing heat exhaustion to worsen into heat stroke. That can lead to altered consciousness, seizures and organ damage, putting life at risk.
If symptoms appear, do not keep pushing yourself. Move to a cool place immediately, loosen your clothes and cool your body down. If the person is fully conscious, drinking water or an electrolyte drink in small amounts can help. But if consciousness becomes clouded, the body temperature is high, or speech and behavior seem unusual, heat stroke should be suspected. In that case, do not force the person to drink water. Call 119 immediately and seek prompt treatment.
◇The basics of preventing heat-related illness are 'water, shade and rest'... Prepare before you feel thirsty
Heat exhaustion occurs due to dehydration and electrolyte loss from heavy sweating, and it can cause fatigue, dizziness, nausea and low blood pressure. Heat cramps are caused by abnormal muscle contractions resulting from salt loss in the body, and cramps usually appear in the arms, legs or abdominal muscles.
If these symptoms appear, stop activity immediately, rest in a cool place and drink fluids containing electrolytes to aid recovery. If heat cramps occur, gently massaging or stretching the affected muscles can help relieve the symptoms.
However, even these mild heat-related illnesses can progress to heat stroke if left untreated. If symptoms last more than an hour or do not improve, you should visit a medical facility for treatment. In particular, high-risk groups such as older adults, people with chronic illnesses and infants and young children can deteriorate even from mild symptoms, so early response is crucial.
To prevent heat-related illness, drink water frequently before you feel thirsty and reduce outdoor activities and work during the hottest hours of the day. When going outside, it is best to wear light-colored, loose-fitting clothes and block the sun with a hat or parasol. If you must be outdoors, take enough breaks in cool places and check yourself often for warning signs such as headache, dizziness or nausea.
Heat-related illness can occur not only outdoors but also indoors if cooling and ventilation are insufficient. During prolonged heat waves, air conditioners and fans should be used properly to keep indoor temperatures from rising too high. Older adults, children and people with chronic illnesses need especially careful attention from family members and those around them because their ability to regulate body temperature is weaker and their risk of dehydration is higher. If symptoms appear, move to a cool place immediately and cool the body down. If symptoms continue even after rest and hydration, or if consciousness becomes clouded, seek medical care without delay.
Kim Jeong-yun emphasized, "Heat-related illness can be prevented, but if you dismiss the symptoms and try to endure them, they can worsen quickly," adding, "On hot days, it is most important to check your condition often and get out of the heat immediately if you feel any unusual symptoms."
